title: Faith
hookLine: the first theological virtue: trust in God, a gift that grows

cards: A father has brought his sick son to Jesus's disciples, and they couldn't help. Now Jesus is here, and the father says, if thou canst do any thing, help us. Jesus picks up that little word if.

All things are possible, he says, to him that believeth. And the father, in Mark's Gospel, cries out with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Belief and unbelief in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy.
A new stretch begins: three gifts Christian teachers call the theological virtues. The first in Paul's list is the one the father was holding onto with both hands.

teach.b: Paul names the three together at the end of his passage on love, which day 89 met: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three."
Christian teachers came to call them theological virtues, because they're aimed at God, and tradition says they're given by God rather than built by effort alone.
The Greek word the New Testament uses for faith, pistis, also means trust. Faith here is less a list of ideas you sign and more a hand you put in someone else's.
The letter to the Hebrews puts it this way: "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." And it's called a gift.
Ephesians says: "by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Christians read that weight differently.

Lutheran and Reformed churches tend to stress that last line: through faith, a gift, not earned. Catholic and Orthodox churches tend to stress, with Galatians, faith which worketh by love. Both read both verses.

In Luke's Gospel the apostles ask Jesus, "Increase our faith." He answers that faith even as small as a grain of mustard seed could tell a tree to be uprooted and planted in the sea. Which brings us back to the father.
He didn't wait until his doubt was gone. He brought it along, said so out loud, and asked for help with it. In the story, that was enough to begin.

how: Christians speak of faith as trust in God that is given and grows; in some churches they profess it together in a creed on Sundays, and some pray the father's words from Mark 9:24 or the apostles' 'increase our faith' in hard moments.

o: being certain, with no questions left at all
a feeling of calm that comes from good luck
trust in God, a gift that can grow alongside doubt

p: the evidence of things not seen

s: in the Gospels, faith means having no doubts at all
the father says "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," and Jesus heals his son.

games.q: you're the father. Jesus has just said all things are possible to him that believeth, and you know your own heart is divided. what do you say?
o: I believe completely; I have no doubts.
Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
nothing; you walk away until your doubt is gone.
games.why: he says both at once, with tears, and Jesus heals the boy. the story honors honest faith that asks for help.

practice: Find one worry you've been carrying in a closed fist, a child, a test result, money, a decision, name it plainly, and slowly open your hands on your knees, palms up.
If you pray, you can hand it over in the father's words, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief; if you don't, just let your hands stay open and notice what it's like not to grip.

wordCard.voice: Faith. In the New Testament's Greek, pistis: trust in God. Christians call it a gift, and something that can grow.

orig.note: Greek: faith, trust, the word used throughout the New Testament for faith.

carryVoice: Your line: trust. Doubt is allowed to come along. I'll be here tomorrow.
